utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would the Registrar call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor v Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann and I appear with Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Fila and I appear for the Defence of Mr. Dokmanovic with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Thank you. As you see, we have kept our promise to hold a hearing today. We were excused by our President from attending our plenary session so we can work here the whole day. However, we have to take account of some other constraints, namely, the fact that another Trial Chamber also will hold a hearing, so we agreed with the Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber 1, Judge Jorda, that we should stop at 1 o'clock and if we need to continue, we can only resume at 4 o'clock pm so that Trial Chamber 1 can hold its hearings at 2.30, from 2.30 to 4. I hope this is convenient to you. Before we call the witness, I would like to ask Mr. Fila whether he could specify a point which I forgot to raise with him, namely, whether sooner or later, he is in a position to tell us how Defence witnesses need to be heard by means of video-conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will provide you with an answer in writing, but before that, I need an answer from Mr. Niemann, whether he has accepted this. One of these witnesses to be heard via video link will appear. If it is shown that Mr. Dokmanovic was not at all at Ovcara, he will not need to appear at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In due time, we will be told so that we -- I think, we hear the technicians can make the necessary preparation, and also I think we need to issue an Order for this purpose so therefore we should know in advance. I think we are now in a position to hear the witness. The Prosecutor may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor would call Stjepan Mesic. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Mesic. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. STJEPAN MESIC

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And where are you from originally in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born at Orahovica in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In 1965, did you run for political office in Orahovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1965 I ran in the elections on the citizen's ticket and I was elected to the Croatian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the same time, did you seek another position or were you elected to another position as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that, I was elected an alderman at the Municipal Assembly and I was also elected President of the Municipal Assembly of Orahovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You indicated that you ran on a ticket other than that of the Communist Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the citizen's ticket. Actually there was the legal possibility then, in addition to the list of candidates which was proposed by the Socialist Alliance and/or the League of Communists, it was also possible for a group of citizens of 100 people to have a candidate run on their behalf and that list, that ticket would become official. Prior to me, nobody did that. I was the first and the last one actually who availed himself of that legal opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the late 1960s, did you become involved in a movement which was known as the Croatian Spring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The movement called the Croatian Spring was a multi-layered movement. It consisted of a part of a League of Communists, the progressive section of the League of Communists of Croatia, the students' movement, the youth movement, the movement comprising university professors and the Martitska Hravadska, which is the cultural society of Croatia, a cultural organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What were the participants in the Croatian Spring movement advocating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the only thing one could have advocated and the thing we did advocate was the greater democratisation in the society, clean accounts in the state, which meant that we were supposed to ascertain in Yugoslavia what was paying for what and who was paying that, why was that being paid for. We advocated the resolution of the foreign exchange system. We advocated the democratisation of society. We wanted it to be possible for people to function normally, to travel normally. At that time, the possibility was still constrained of travelling abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the reaction of Tito to the Croatian Spring movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, Tito supported us. He came to Zagreb. He even encouraged the Croatian Spring movement, but when the generals had deciphered Croatian Spring as a nationalistic movement, then characterised it as such, Tito accepted what was demanded of him from the army and he asked that all those who had participated in that movement be removed from politics, and also that they be ousted from their professional posts so that at the meeting in Kragujevac and the 21st session of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia started, I can freely say, the persecution of the participants in the Croatian Spring, which included myself and another 10,000 people and the 10,000 people or even more ended in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you removed from your positions as President of the Municipality and from your seat in the Sabor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I and everybody else were removed from our positions and I was practically left in the street and could not find employment for two years. Although I had been admitted to the bar, I could not practise my profession as an attorney. I could not hold any public office for that matter, so that until the time when I was to serve my prison sentence, I actually did not work. I only found short term ad hoc employment until they found out who I was and then I would be let off, so it lasted. I was sentenced to two years and two months and I spent my prison sentence in Stara Gradiska prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Upon your release, were you able to find employment at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not able to find employment. But it so happened that an engineer, Zarko Vincek was his name, he was heading a consulting firm and he had been in the ranks of the partisans, together with my father. He of course did not consider himself no more than I did a nationalist, so that he gave me a job, so in fact after he left, I got to be the manager of the firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: As a result of the Croatian Spring movement, were some changes made by Tito in the structure of the Yugoslav government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I believe that Tito's latest options were greatly influenced, in fact, by the ideas of the Croatian Spring movement, but also by the ideas of liberalism in Serbia, which is why he indeed proceeded to amend the constitution and have a new one adopted in 1974, which introduced into the Yugoslav mechanism a confederal model. He intended thereby to create such a system of decision-making in Yugoslavia where there would be a -- at the top a Presidency which would bring all the most important decisions by consensus, and the Members of the Presidency would rotate to hold the presidential and vice-presidential functions following an automatic mechanism, and he thought that after his demise and the disappearance of his charisma, Yugoslavia would be able to function too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How many members were there in the Presidency as set out in the new constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the new constitution, there were eight members of the Presidency, two representing the provinces, the others representing the republics, with practically that constitution making the provinces -- conferring upon the provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo the status of a state which was not acceptable to the Serbian leadership, so that immediately after the adoption of the 1974 constitution, they raised objections, vociferous objections, to that particular constitutional arrangement. I mean, coming from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After Tito's death in 1981, did the system function in the way that he had envisaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a time the system did function by virtue of its very inertia. However, more and more conflicts came to the fore and were experienced because of different clashing interests in the different levels of development of the different republics. Some were dissatisfied because they were just the raw materials, the resource base and their raw materials were sold at markets at lower prices than was the case at the world markets. The other parts, the more developed parts were not content because they had to pay for the less developed parts, various contributions, which then exhausted their own economies, of those republics, and, secondly, the problem which was there obviously was that this top-heavy mechanism of the army exhausted the country, it swallowed up very extensive resources and that also led to conflicts among the republics and conflicts of interests among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did Slobodan Milosevic come to power in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic assumed the power -- I cannot recall the exact year, but some two or three years prior to these democratic changes. He was consolidated practically in his seat of power by the so-called rallying of the people. The conflicts in Kosovo actually threw him out on the surface, because practically what he intended to do was to destroy the autonomy of Kosovo, of the province which actually later events demonstrated. After everything which had transpired in Kosovo and Vojvodina, one could see the true face of Slobodan Milosevic and his actual intention which was that Serbia had to be whole and could not consist of three parts and this is an idea which he systematically pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the anti-bureaucratic revolution which occurred under Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard for me to assist on that from the angle of Croatia, but I believe that it was a farce, a travesty. It was just a power struggle and they were supposed to oust the old echelons, the Tito-oriented old structuring and the pro Yugoslav echelons. New structures were to be installed instead to accept Milosevic's totalitarian authority and power and this is what he indeed implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the Yoghurt Revolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yoghurt Revolution is the name given to that phase of the anti-bureaucratic revolution which was waged in Vojvodina that -- because in Vojvodina that the leadership that was in power was in favour of autonomy and it consisted of people who were not burdened by any sort of nationalism and who bothered Milosevic so that he brought loyal people, people loyal to him, but mainly people who were not natives of Vojvodina that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was Milosevic also able to affect a change in the leadership in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was, because the Montenegrin authorities, the leadership was also pro Yugoslav in their orientation and when I analysed Milosevic, he was really never interested in any Yugoslavia, be it federal or confederal. The only thing that he was interested in was a Greater Serbia and that was his basic objective. Namely, the first demands raised by the so-called anti-bureaucratic revolution were that Yugoslavia had to be reconstructed, that Serbia had only received damage within Yugoslavia and clearly that the autonomies had to disappear and that only later -- and only later, when he implemented all of this, when he had implemented all of this, he -- because of the Croatian factors, was ostensibly advocating the country's -- Serbia's remaining in the whole Yugoslavia, whereas he was doing everything to the country to dismantle it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago that Mr. Milosevic had taken some steps against Kosovo. What happened to the Assembly in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic ousted the entire leadership in Kosovo. He abolished the Kosovo Assembly and this travesty went so far as to have the representative of Kosovo come and sit in the Presidency of Yugoslavia and was elected by the Serbian Assembly to sit in the Presidency, because the Kosovo Assembly never met any more, never convened any more, and of course, as far as I know, the population of Kosovo is 90 per cent Albanian, and the rest are Serbs. Obviously he disregarded this altogether and he abolished its autonomy. First the federal organ started with this exercise of pacifying Kosovo and then that role was assumed by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Over time, was Milosevic able to effect a change in the autonomous status of both Kosovo and Vojvodina and if so, was this formalised in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, nobody actually asked Kosovo or Vojvodina that, because ultimately, they did not participate in any elections any more. The constitution was adopted of the Republic of Serbia which practically abolished the autonomies of both provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On June 28th 1989, Milosevic made a speech at Gazimestan in Kosovo in which he spoke about Serbia's relations with its neighbours. Do you recall what, if anything, he said in terms of the possibility of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that was a turning point for the entire political space of the Former Yugoslavia, because Milosevic said, I do not remember the exact formulation, he said that they had quarrels and conflicts in the area of Yugoslavia and that those battles were not yet armed ones, but that one was not to rule out the possibility of armed battles being waged as well. Then there were great rallies of people being organised throughout Serbia who were very much in the mood to continue this trend which arose in Kosovo and Vojvodina and the rest of Serbia to sort of have it spill over to the rest of Yugoslavia, and this instilled great fear throughout the country, including in Croatia, and in fact resulted with the League of Communists, or the top leadership of the League of Communists in Croatia, deciding to hold early elections so that whosoever should win those elections should be supported by the people and be in a position to organise a defence because those threats ceased being only verbal threats. It was a threat which actually made our blood run cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In early 1990, when the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia was held, did any splits develop within the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this Congress is especially important because it marked the stop of factor of integration, the existence of a factor of integration, namely, Yugoslavia could exist until -- as long as it had three integrated factors: first of all, Tito with his charisma, the second factor was the League of Communists, the Communist Party, and the third was the Yugoslav Army which was also a general Yugoslav entity. With the demise of Tito, two factors remained and with the disintegration of the League of Communists, there remained just one factor and that was the Yugoslav Army, so it seems to me that it was a deliberate action on the part of Milosevic to destroy that factor so that he himself could assume control -- I mean, the second factor -- so that he in fact could assume control. The third factor: the Yugoslav Army, which as time showed, he gradually turned from a Yugoslav into a Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the absence of a centralised Yugoslav Communist Party, did the Communist Party, at the republic level, increase in power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in fact the Communists in both Slovenia and Croatia started thinking in a different way. They started advocating a multi-party system, because they felt that the monopoly of power of the League of Communists was untenable and there were sweeping democratic changes elsewhere in the world and this also came to expression in our parts, so that soon thereafter, the parties were in fact inaugurated following the European model.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have said that the communist parties particularly in Croatia and Slovenia were advocating a multi-party system. Did this lead to free elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is precisely that possibility, rather, this lack of fear of a multi-party system is something that came into being through an evolution. New people came forward and they realised that belonging to different parties does not mean that people are enemies. It simply means that they think differently about different problems. That is why they allowed this multi-party system to be inaugurated. First, it went very slowly, but afterwards, we got real political parties, precisely due to these developments that were taking place, and also the development of democratic thought within the ranks of the League of Communists of Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the elections which occurred in April and May of 1990 in Croatia, did you participate as a candidate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I started to work in the Croatian democratic community together with Franjo Tudjman, Josip Manolic, Josip Bowkovac and I was a candidate in the same place where I was a candidate in 1965 and I was elected to the Croatian Parliament for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have referred to this party as the Croatian Democratic Union. Is it commonly referred to as the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is not called a party. It is called a union, because there was a danger involved that when new parties were established, the regime could prevent them, forbid them, because the law forbade the establishment of political parties. Various interest groups could be established. Politics is also a group of interests, but this was not fully defined by law. So in order to avoid this legal trap, the HDZ was formed as a union and that is the name that remained. However, the HDZ did not fully come into being as a party. It remained a movement, but a few parties were established in Croatia which are well defined, which have been operating and certainly functioning within this political environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have indicated that you individually were elected to Parliament. How did the HDZ fare overall in the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ won those elections thanks to the law which made it possible to have a relative majority and yet win the largest number of seats in the Croatian Parliament. I became the first Prime-Minister Designate of the first government of Croatia, so I became the Premier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At some point in May of 1990, did you become aware of the formation in Knin of an Association of Serb Municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about this action. I think it was wrong, because the Serb population in Croatia was thus put into a ghetto and I think that it was a harmful decision, harmful for Croatia as a whole and harmful to Serbs within Croatia as the citizens of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Who formed this organisation, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The political organisation SDS. The Serb Democratic Party, was established by Dr. Jovan Raskovic, who was the ideological leader of the party too. However, I think it was Milan Babic who proclaimed this community and he was President of the Municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During your tenure as Prime Minister, did you ever make attempts to establish a dialogue with representatives of the predominantly Serb municipalities in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As political parties developed, but also as general developments took place, the SDS was established with a strong nationalist feeling, but then on the other hand there were also Croatian parties with similar ideas. So there was tension and all of this resulted in roadblocks. This was called the Log Revolution later on, so Croatian roads and railroads became inoperative. The economy came to a standstill. Practically it was chaos, because it was impossible to have the state function if roads and railroads were cut off. In my capacity as Prime Minister, I asked for talks with the Presidents of the municipalities that became part of this Community of Municipalities. I must say in all fairness that all the Presidents of Municipalities agreed with this meeting and I was pleased with that, and I said that we could meet anywhere in Plitvice, in Zagreb, at the seaside, wherever it was convenient for them, so that we could see what the problems were and how we could together work out these problems. It is only the President of the Municipality of Knin, Milan Babic, that did not respond to my investigation. He sent his -- the Secretary of his Municipality. He said that he personally accepts this and he thinks that it is a good idea to sit down and talk and to bring these tensions to a halt, to bring all our problems to the negotiating table and to see how we can resolve them, and I said, "What about President Babic, the President of the Municipality?" He said that he was in Belgrade and that he would call me back as soon as he got back from Belgrade. Because he did not call me back, I asked for a meeting again within a couple of days. Again, it is the Secretary of the Municipality who talked to me and he said that Milan Babic prohibited all Presidents of Municipalities from keeping in any kind of contact with the government of Zagreb. Of course, after that, it was difficult to establish communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In August of 1990, did something occur whereby Croatia lost control of the police station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it. Part of the police force abandoned the force in an organised fashion by taking over the police station in Knin and cutting off all contacts and all communication with the Ministry of the Interior. Of course, this was an example to other municipalities as well and similar things occurred elsewhere too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was an attempt made at any point by the Croatian police to retake control of this station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to retake control of the police station, fast action was needed and one of the ways of doing this was to establish police stations in neighbouring towns and villages, so that the renegade police from Knin could not operate in the entire area. In Kijevo, which is near Knin, a police station was established. Also, there was a proposal, an attempt made to establish this kind of control. We sent three helicopters with police escorts to get into Knin and establish this kind of control. However, the Mig aircraft of the Yugoslav Army stopped these helicopters and this action failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the rationale of the JNA in intervening in this manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I was taken by surprise by this action of the JNA, but also by their explanations. Namely, it would have been logical for the army to support officialdom, the Ministry of the Interior. They were taking normal action to re-establish law and order in the state and it only would have been natural for them to support that kind of action. However, they prevented that from happening and it was very difficult for me to get the telephone number of General Blagoja Adzic. I called him and I protested. Why are Yugoslav Mig aircraft stopping the action of a legal police which has to re-establish control over its territory? He was very arrogant. He said that every attempt to take police by helicopters to Knin would be thwarted and if one Serb head were to fall, 2,000 Croat heads would fall and I was really surprised to hear something like that from a Yugoslav general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you know at that time what his position was in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1990, did your position in government change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the autumn of 1990, the Croat political leadership came to the conclusion that the newly established democratic government in Croatia would have to have its own representative in the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Until then, Stipe Suva was a Member of this Presidency as the representative of Croatia. I was chosen. The Croatian Parliament elected me and I was sent to Belgrade, first, to be Vice-President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and after that, there was an automatic change involved, meaning that I would become eventually President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When you entered the Presidency, who were the other members at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, the Representative of Kosovo was Riza Sapundziu; the Representative of Vojvodina was Professor Zelenovic; the Representative of Slavonia, Dr. Janez Drnovsek; the Representative of Macedonia was Dr. Vasil Tupurkovski; the Representative of Bosna-Herzegovina, Bogic Bogicevic; the Representative of Serbia was Borisav Jovic and the Representative of Montenegro was Nenad Bucin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, did some of the membership change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a change. Professor Dr. Riza Sapundziu was replaced by Cedo Bajramovic who was elected by the Serbian Assembly on behalf of the autonomous province of Kosovo, namely, the Kosovo Parliament never met again so the Serbian Parliament recalled Riza Sapundziu and brought Cedo Bajramovic to this place and I think he did not even speak Albanian; at least I never heard him utter a word in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What about the representatives from Montenegro and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A representative of Montenegro was Nenad Bucin. Later on, rather, when Borisav Jovic, the Representative of Serbia, withdrew from the Presidency, Nenad Bucin did too. He also resigned. However, Borisav Jovic went back to the Presidency, but Nenad Bucin kept his word and he did not go back to the Presidency, so he was replaced by Branko Kostic from Montenegro. I think that Zelenovic went to a post that was incompatible, so to speak, so Yugoslav Kostic took his place here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you aware of an initiative which was undertaken by Martin Spegelj during 1990 to secure weapons for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was not only the initiative of Martin Spegelj. Croatia was fully disarmed before the first democratic elections. The Yugoslav National Army took all the weapons of the Territorial Defence, namely, the system was such that the operative army was under the command of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the Territorial Defence, its entire system, was under the command of the Republic and therefore the Republic also took care of the financial resources needed, so it was the President of the Republic that was in command. Just before the elections, all these weapons of the Territorial Defence were taken. The police force was poorly armed. There were 15,000 policemen with small arms and the decision was that, in view of all the dangers that were looming over Croatia, that Croatia should, within the Ministry of the Interior, set up a formation which was called the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, which was like a gendarmerie, as the French have, that it should involve a military set-up, but they should be run by the Ministry of the Interior. So in other words to carry out this kind of reorganisation, the Ministry of the Interior asked the federal ministry for a permit to buy weapons within Yugoslavia. However, we received their answer saying that there were no weapons and the factory -- the weapons manufacturing factory of Zastava Crvena could not sell us weapons. After that, the Ministry of the Interior made a decision in keeping with the law that weapons should be bought outside Yugoslavia and they were bought. Of course, not in the quantities that were the subject of speculation afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 9th January 1991, at the meeting of the Presidency, did some discussion take place regarding the disarming of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was debate, because the Yugoslav Army was arming Serb villages, which was a suicidal policy, in my opinion, because arming 10 per cent of the Croatian population that was Serb, ran against Serbian interests, but unfortunately the Yugoslav Army was doing that consistently. Regrettably, Croats were getting arms on the other hand too. We had the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, also the police force, which got some more serious weapons at this stage, but then there were also some groups that were outside of this framework and therefore there was a discussion about this, that illegal paramilitary organisations should be disarmed, and the Presidency agreed with this of course. All those organisations that were not under the command of the Ministry of the Interior were illegal. The ZNG, the National Guards Corps, was a legal organisation, so this disarmament did not apply to the ZNG and there was a conflict of opinions on this particular matter, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 21st January, do you recall a telephone conversation you had from Sarajevo with Borosav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I was in Sarajevo. I gave a lecture there and Borosav Jovic found me there. That is where I first met Radovan Karadzic, so I was surprised by his views too. Borosav Jovic asked me to agree to some of his proposals, but I could not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the 25th January 1991 meeting of the Presidency, did discussion take place in relation to the intervention of the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were actually the proposals of Borosav Jovic and I voted against using the army. However, the promise was that the army would not intervene, that it would only appear and that by their very appearance, they would stop the revolt that had exploded in the streets of Belgrade, so I was against this and I voted against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what was the vote within the Presidency at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By a majority of votes, it was accepted that the army could appear, but that they could not intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure if we are speaking of the same thing. I am talking about the point at which there was discussion about the JNA intervening in Croatia and I think this was your response, you had indicated about the demonstrations in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. Yes, I was wrong. In Croatia, the army never got the right to go out of barracks, namely, this was a special situation when there would be a conflict with certain renegade groups that were taking larger and larger territory. It was a public secret simply that on the territory of Croatia, a Serb state was being established which was unacceptable for Croatia, but the army was arming all these groups and then when there was a conflict, the Army would come out and cover the area and prevent any kind of communication with the official government of Croatia. That is to say, that the army was already outside and we could not take that army back. I mean, we who were opposed to using the army, could not make the army do this. We could not get a majority in the Presidency which would vote in favour of this kind of an order. There was a blockade. It was four against four. On the one hand, there was the so-called Serb bloc, Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo and Vojvodina and on the other hand, was Bosna-Herzegovina, Croatia, Slovenia and Macedonia, so there was this racial four to four, so we could not vote in favour of withdrawing the army, but what we could pass as a decision was that the army should withdraw within three months and that that was the deadline by which the army would have to go back to their barracks. So this was accepted, I imagine, because the Representatives of Serbia and the top echelons of the Army thought that they would crush all resistance within that three-month period and establish the kind of situation they wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When did that occur, that the army went out for this three-month period? Was there some event that preceded that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Pakrac. It was Plitvice, especially in Pakrac, the army was out for no reason and the Presidency had not passed any decision on the Army in this relation and in Pakrac, the renegades had attacked the police station. The Minister of the Interior had established a unit, a detachment, that went there and disarmed these people who were in the police station. In the police station there were some policemen and after that the army came with their tanks, with a large number of tanks. They came from different sides and I was in Zagreb at that point and I decided to go to this very place, so I went to Pakrac. We had talks with the army there. There were four generals, 20 colonels, a total of 70 officers and after that, I had lunch with them too that day. General Vasiljevic, Head of the Counter-Intelligence Service, had organised this entire provocation because the plan was to cut across Croatia, Virovitica along -- along the line between them and that is why there were provocations along that particular line. He had organised that particular provocation but it was not as official as they had wanted it to be. People had not started shooting at each other yet. Vasiljevic claimed that women and children had fled, that they were hiding in forests, that forests were full of people who were fearful of the Croat authorities during the Second World War. I was hiding in the forest too before I went to Hungary. I said, I am personally going to go and see all these people, because there is no reason for anyone to fear anyone in Croatia. Myself least of all, because, after all, 11 members of my family lost their lives while fighting on the partisan side and then General Trifunovic, who is a reasonable man, said, you know what, sir? These are not people who are fleeing and hiding in the forest. This is a farce. There was some shooting, but no one has been wounded. No one has been killed and the whole thing should calm down. It is precisely because of this man and because of some other reasonable officers, that I stayed for lunch with them. The next day, we had a meeting of the Presidency and I informed the other members of the Presidency about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I can just ask you a question very quickly. This General Trifunovic that you spoke with, was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, at the meeting that followed this, did you have any conversations with Borosav Jovic about the casualties that had occurred in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I knew exactly what was happening in Pakrac and I was able to inform the Members of the Presidency about what had been happening, that it had been a provocation, that people were not shooting at one another. There were obvious traces of shooting on the buildings, but there were no casualties, no one was wounded, no one was killed. Later, Borosav Jovic told me at this meeting obviously that he had read in the Titograd paper -- and you can imagine how far Titograd is from Pakrac -- that there had been no denials of the fact, but there could not have been any by that time in fact, that he had read, namely, that 40 Serbs had been massacred at Pakrac. I told him that that was a total inexactitude -- misinformation, that he was supposed to believe me and not something possibly written by the popular paper of Titograd which was being printed some, I believe, 800 kilometres away from the scene of the event and that he should not believe things that had not been denied. I told him, okay, if you believe that, then you can believe anything which I myself read in the paper, and no one has denied it. Namely, in the Mladina, the paper from Ljubljana, I read that Slobodan Milosevic had schizophrenia, but I do not believe it, although no one had denied it. So there was a sort of a silence which ensued, confused silence if you will, and then after that, my report about what was happening in Pakrac was indeed accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time period in March of 1991, February and March, who was the President of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borosav Jovic was the President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At that point in time, was he the Commander in-Chief of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was and I myself was the Vice-President, because, according to the rules of procedure and the law which regulated the operation of the Presidency, there was an automatic mechanism under which the previous Vice-President would take the place of the former President and that was an automatic mechanism, so we rotated in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: A little earlier you mentioned demonstrations in Belgrade. Did a meeting ensue in the Presidency in early March to discuss this issue and where a request was made for intervention of troops on the streets in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely why I sort of contradicted myself, because it was precisely Borosav Jovic who asked me by telephone whether I was in favour of the army coming out into the streets and I did not accept that. That decision was taken by a majority of Croats, but I myself did not vote in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the following meeting of the Presidency on 12th March, which occurred at the army Headquarters; how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Decisions of the Presidency were legally held in the Palace of the Federation in the presidential rooms and there were no difficulties associated with that whatsoever. When we convened that particular session to which I came, on the 12th, before the actual session, we came there, a military bus waited for us with an escort of officers there, because they told us that we would have to go to the staff of the Supreme Command to hold that meeting because they had all the necessary maps from which we could get an insight into the situation then obtaining in Yugoslavia, so, in order not to take all of that material to the Presidency, it would be much better for us to meet there, so we did go and that was sort of a construction, if you will. We came. We took our winter greatcoats off, but the room in which we were to hold the session was not heated, so they offered us Army greatcoats to wear, to all of us, so that we were turned, in a way, into soldiers, and perhaps that was supposed also to have a certain influence, bearing on the decision-making. The majority of us did not accept that and we endured throughout the session. Later, I saw the session. It was videotaped and I saw it on the BBC. I am not sure how they obtained that material. It was a tumultuous session indeed and in a certain sense, it was a turning point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this meeting in regard to discussions about the JNA intervention in Croatia, was anything decided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the army insisted and not once when I saw the army, it was always the Minister of Defence of Yugoslavia, Veljko Kadijevic and his Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav general staff, Blagoja Adzic. They were always asking for, including at that session, with all possible explanations, that the army was to be given carte blanche, that it was the army that should of itself decide what action to take and that that should be covered by the Presidency decision, but that the army should be left to decide the timing and the actual action to be undertaken by the army. I remember that at the entrance I met Bogic Bogicevic, the Representative of Bosna-Herzegovina and someone told me -- I believe it was Tuperkoski -- that they had talked the whole night, that the generals had talked to Bogic Bogicevic all night, and I asked him how he felt after having talked so pleasantly to the generals all that night and he said, "Well, fine." Then I asked him, "How are we going to fare at the session?" He said, "You know that I am a man of principle", and when we came to the vote, we knew, more or less, what the outcome would be, how the people would vote, but the army thought that by exerting pressure on Bogic Bogicevic because he was a Serb, they would win him over to their proposal, the proposal of the Serbian leadership. Borisav Jovic was so surprised by the vote cast by Bogic Bogicevic, that he said, "Look here, you are a Serb", but he said, "Yes, but first of all, I am a Bosnian. So this decision was not carried because the ratio was 4 to 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: When the Presidency failed to vote -- to allow the army, as you said, carte blanche in Croatia, what was the reaction, if any, of Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadijevic was quite nervous and although he tried to pretend since the time we came, a sort of intimacy, a feigned intimacy, he looked quite, shall I say, well in the mood -- in a good mood, when we came, but as discussions advanced, and especially after what I had said, he was quite furious. Namely, after we came to that session, after they had brought us to that session, I had a question to ask, because I wanted to know what kind of a discussion I would have to conduct. The question was: was I under arrest or was I not under arrest, because I had come under military escort and on a military bus, so I said: if I am under arrest, I have this sort of a discussion to say and state, and if I am not, I will have a different story to tell. This infuriated General Kadijevic greatly. After that, he was unable to restrain himself, to calm down, and after the voting was over, he ran out of the room, but he did come back and I was again surprised when he said that the army would act only upon the basis of the constitution and its constitutional responsibilities. That the Presidency obviously -- that he did not want to have anything to do with that Presidency, but after he came back, I am not quite sure, after 20 -- 15 or 20 minutes, he said that he thought that Serbia would found its own Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the following days, did there come an occasion when Borosav Jovic resigned from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately, the second day after that, Borosav Jovic tendered his written resignation, but he spoke on television and he said that he would not be coming to the Presidency any more after the failure by the Presidency to take the decision demanded from it by the military leaders. I myself also spoke on television shortly thereafter and I said that nothing special had happened, that the President had resigned and that I had taken over assuming all the state functions and duties and that the state mechanisms would continue to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 16th March, did Slobodan Milosevic make a public statement regarding what he saw as the status of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is a statement which I believe led to a total turning point in relations in Yugoslavia. Namely, Slobodan Milosevic said that those were the last days of the Yugoslav agony, that Serbia, as Borosav Jovic has withdrawn from the Presidency, would not be delegating anyone else to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, but also that Serbia would not be bound any more by any decisions whatsoever of the Presidency. In other words, he was announcing secession and that decision of his had never been revoked, although after a certain period of time, Borosav Jovic did appear at the session and pretended that nothing had happened. However, as regards Milosevic, his decision to the effect that Serbia would not be bound by the President's decision was something that he never publicly revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did Milosevic at the same time make any statements regarding mobilisation of the Serbian Territorial Defence or militia forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He immediately announced mobilisation which clearly -- he said, total mobilisation of all special forces, reserve forces in Serbia, and those reserve force members later appeared throughout the soil of Croatia and clearly this had an effect on the homogenisation, in the defensive sense, of peoples on the other parts of the Yugoslav soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was Slobodan Milosevic's position at this time in March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the President of Serbia and clearly, on the basis of the decision of his own Assembly, he was able to conduct a mobilisation. However, he had no such decision of his Assembly and, regrettably, the Army was also drafting people, although the Presidency had never taken any decision to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you able to determine if Slobodan Milosevic had any influence on the manner in which Borosav Jovic and the other members of the Serbian bloc voted in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite obvious that the military leaders were under the influence and the direct control of Slobodan Milosevic and they did not even make that a secret. Namely, not a single general -- and I can say that now -- not a single general of the Yugoslav Army ever came to my office, to the office of his Commander in-Chief, because I was not then at the helm of the Presidency and thereby in a way, I was the Commander in-Chief of the Yugoslav Army. So not a single one of these generals ever came to see me, seeing that the situation became more and more complicated, and tragically so in fact, because the human casualties became enormous and the devastation of property became enormous, I tried to do something about it to calm matters down and I sought to talk to the Minister of Defence, Veljko Kadijevic. I tried to persuade him that the army should not interfere in political arrangements, because that was actually marring the situation. The army was actually drawing the boundaries of the Greater Serbia and that obviously was their mission. What I told General Kadijevic, when I asked him, actually, why was he so much influenced by Slobodan Milosevic, the President of Serbia, he said that he did not have such a great influence, but that he was cooperating with him, because everybody else was greater, bigger, Chetniks, than Slobodan Milosevic and he was the only one that he could contact, cooperate with in Serbia, but I told him: look, can you not see that Slobodan Milosevic, it is quite clear, is creating a Serbian Army and that he will not be needing Yugoslav, but only Serbian officers, and once his mission is completed, he will leave his post. Then he told me, "As long as I live", but I told him, "Look, if you oppose Milosevic, you will not live, because the army started dissipating and people, Croats and Slovaks and Bosnians and Muslims, they were all leaving the army -- Albanians were leaving the army -- so that that increasingly was becoming a Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I had also asked about the influence that Milosevic had in terms of the mobs of the Presidency, Borosav Jovic and the other members that you described of this Serbian bloc. Did he have influence over the way in which they voted in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct, Borosav Jovic was controlling these two or rather three members of his, the Representatives of Montenegro, Kosovo and Vojvodina, whereas he himself, whenever any votes were taken, would leave the room for a bit. He would go outside and at the exit, I was -- I would always say to him, "Borosav, give my regards to Milosevic, and transact your business as quickly as possible so that we can really get down to the voting." That is what he actually did. He would come back then and complete his task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the same time as Milosevic's statement on 16th March, did some type of declaration come out of Knin in regard to the Serb-held areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was obviously a synchronised exercise. No one was surprised by it. Namely, Babic had proclaimed his secession from Croatia and thereby no longer recognised any authority of Zagreb. That was secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Earlier you had mentioned that some events had occurred at Plitvice. What exactly had happened there at the end of March of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What had happened was that, precisely this, renegade authorities had taken control over Plitvice. The Ministry of Defence wanted to return the police station to this spot and to re-establish the normal functioning of all authorities of all bodies, including the functioning of the Plitvice compound and as well as of the adjacent municipalities. It was obvious that there had been no reason for an armed conflict and it is obvious also because the policemen who were there normally doing their routine, duties, came on a bus without any special security forces. But they were met there with fire from machine-guns, automatic guns. The first lives were lost; Josip Jovic, a policeman, was killed on that occasion. After that, the situation deteriorated further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were any of the Serbs who had been involved in the taking of this station in Plitvice arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several people were taken into custody, among whom Goran Hadzic, who just happened to be there, although there is actually not a single reason, there was not a single reason for him to be there, because he is from the Podunavlje area. I believe that later he was either exchanged or liberated or he just was travelling through the area and happened to be there in a room with another priest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Podunavlje area which you have referred to, is that more commonly known as Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Eastern Slavonia and Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: After Plitvice, was the JNA given some latitude by the Presidency to act in Croatia for a three-month period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Presidency took no decision, giving any sort of powers to the Yugoslav Army. The Yugoslav Army actually was in a limbo, without a decision of the Presidency and it was there on a certain spot and because it could not be returned, we said, "Let them stay where they are", and so they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where they were at that point in time was out of barracks; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were out of barracks and up to that moment, they were there actually, I think, totally illegally, but after that moment, they could not undertake any further illegal action, but they could remain for another three months where they had found themselves, until the deadline prescribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Also in late March, did you become aware of a meeting which took place between Slobodan Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman at Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only did I become aware of that meeting, but in the end, I turned out to be some kind of an organiser of that meeting, not specifically in the composition which they convened; namely, I told Borosav Jovic as the Representative of Serbia in the state Presidency, that we had heard, that we had in fact -- that the garrisons of the Yugoslav armies were arming Serbs with highly sophisticated weapons, not only defensive weaponry, and that there was the possibility that a conflict would ensue and that there was a possibility that it could escalate to certain proportions and that also the Croats would arm themselves, that everything will get out of hand. In a conflict of population of 10 per cent of Serbs with the rest of 90 per cent being Croats, the greatest loser, I told him, would be the Serbs in Croatia. They would remain without everything. They would lose their property and they would lose their lives. So I asked him, "Why are you pushing people into such a suicidal act when everything can be settled at the table and we can take all the problems one by one, address them one by one and see how to resolve them at the table? Are you interested? Are you interested in Serbs as citizens of Croatia and to that, he told me, "We are not interested in the Serbs in Croatia. They are your citizens. You do with them whatever you feel like. You can impale them on the stake if you want. It is not our problem. It is your problem". I asked him, "What about the territory?" He told me, "We are not interested in Croatian territory. We are interested in 66 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that used to be Serbian, that is Serbian that will remain Serbian. I told him, "If you are not interested in Serbs in Croatia, if you are not interested in Croatian territory and the only problem which you have is Bosnia, let us then sit down at the table and try to find a solution to the problems obtaining in Croatia so as to calm down the tensions, ease the tensions for us to start functioning normally." As for the Bosnian problem, let it be internationalised, let it be resolved through the United Nations, but then again, let us all do that without war." I also told him, "If that is as it is, as you say, do you agree that Tudjman and I myself on the one side, and you and Slobodan Milosevic on the other side, should meet somewhere and try and make an analysis of things and possibly propose a solution?" He told me that he personally agreed, but that he had to hear Milosevic on that score and that he would get back to me in about an hour. Very quickly, he told me that Slobodan Milosevic agreed to such a meeting and that he was in fact proposing that the meeting be held anywhere in the country or abroad. With that view, I went to Zagreb on the same day and I told Tudjman that these two wanted this meeting. I recounted the entire conversation I had and then he told me, "Okay, it is good for me to know that they want to talk and I will tell you when to organise the meeting." However, I was never given -- I never had this occasion to organise that or such a meeting. I only found out when Tudjman said that he would be meeting Slobodan Milosevic, that he would be meeting only Slobodan Milosevic, that the venue of the meeting would be Karadjordjevo, that the reason for the meeting was to see what Milosevic wanted. The reason I objected to that was that there had been a meeting in 1971, held in Karadjordjevo after which meeting we had suffered certain consequences, that many of us had ended up in prison, that it was not the very best of places to be chosen for a meeting with Milosevic. He said, "Look, it does not matter. It is really of no consequence where the meeting is going to be held. I just want to see what he wants. So he went there and he met him alone and he returned on the same day and told me he had been given assurances by the Yugoslav Army that it would not be attacking Croatia, that those guarantees were not being given by only Veljko Kadijevic, but also Slobodan Milosevic. That Bosnia was untenable. That that was the opinion of Slobodan Milosevic and that Croatia in that case would be given the boundaries from 1938 when it was Banovina in 1939, whereby it would nicely round off its territory and that Slobodan Milosevic had also said: you can also take Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac, the so-called Turkish Croatian and Western Bosnia. Serbia does not need it. Then I said I did not find that logical for Milosevic to go to war to dismember Bosnia, that we are faring the best in that case without any war and then ultimately, whether it was at all possible to divide Bosnia without a war, and then he told me that I did not know the historical forces. I said perhaps I do not know historical forces, but time will tell who is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In early May, did an incident occur in Borovo Selo that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the entire public, both home and abroad, found out about this, namely, the Croatian police was following this arming of Serbian villages and a police patrol was following a van that was heavily loaded. They imagined that it was full of arms and they lost sight of it somewhere along the road. As they were looking for this van, they came to the centre of Borovo Selo, fire was opened at them. One person was killed. Another person was wounded -- was arrested, taken prisoner, and a third person managed to escape. He came to Vukovar and said what had happened. And the local police command sent a bus full of policemen there and of course they were not counting on any kind of conflict. They thought that when more policemen showed up, they would manage to restore law and order and to see who was shooting, who was taking armed action when there was no reason for that. However, they were met with heavy fire. 12 policemen were killed. Many were wounded and finally, it was established that many of these assailants had come from Serbia, that they were well armed, that they were professionals, and of course this was a tragic event as far as Croatia was concerned, that people who were doing their job were killed in such a barbarous way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You had been serving as the Vice-President of the Presidency during this period. Was there a particular date on which you were scheduled to rotate into the post of President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was supposed to become President of the Presidency according to that inertia, this automatic change. It was simply supposed to be stated that Croatia had sent its Representative to be President, that his term as Vice-President was expiring and that he was supposed to take over the post of President. This was supposed to take place in March. However, the Serbian bloc disagreed with this and Borosav Jovic had put this to the vote. Until then, everything was automatic in this respect. One person abstained. The vote was four to three and Borosav, as President, said that the President was not elected. This created a vacuum. This is to say, that this automatic change was no longer observed and Serbia insisted that anyone could come from Croatia, but Stjepan Mesic. This was unacceptable and offensive to Croatia because in that way, Serbia would be deciding who would represent Croatia in the Presidency of Yugoslavia. A crisis broke out practically in these overall relations, then the European Community troika came in, that is to say the representatives of the international community, political pressure was brought to bear and they tried to force the Serbian leadership and the Serbian bloc to accept this solution which was not imposed upon Yugoslavia by anyone. This was part of regular practice. After quite a bit of time, I think it was two months, they accepted that I would be President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and I think that the main role in this respect was played by Van den Broek who wanted this decision to be carried through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure if this was a mistranslation or not. In terms of the date when this occurred, was this March or was this in May when you were supposed to become the President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was the fifth -- it was May, sorry. This went on for about two months. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 25th June 1991, did something happen in Croatia and Slovenia of significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Croatia organised a referendum. First, it organised a referendum on what the citizens of Croatia wanted and at that referendum, I think that 94 per cent of the citizens voted in favour of independence. There were two options. One was to remain in Yugoslavia and the other one was for independence. 84 per cent voted for independence. I am just trying to say that the majority of the Serbs also voted for an independent Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was this independence actually declared on 25th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after this referendum, the Croatian Parliament accepted the decision taken by the referendum and proclaimed independence, but I have to say that this was before the proclamation of independence. I mean, Croatia and Slovenia, before the proclamation of independence-- tried or rather the Representatives tried, myself included -- to reconstruct Yugoslavia, because it was quite clear that Yugoslavia, as it was, could not continue to be. All the republics were dissatisfied with their status. They all thought that they were losers in Yugoslavia and this was a sign that this state mechanism had to be reconstructed. Milosevic, as he was toppling Kosovo, Vojvodina and the leadership of Montenegro, he also said that Serbia was harmed by Yugoslavia. He even said that factories in Serbia would be dismantled as after the Second World War and taken elsewhere, and various explanations were given to the effect that Serbia did not need Yugoslavia. After all, we saw this in his decision, that he did not recognise any decisions by the Presidency of Yugoslavia, but when he reinforced his power, when he toppled the provinces and the leadership in Montenegro, then he allegedly started working in favour of Yugoslavia and then he said that Serbia was only interested in a firm federation, and a firm federation meant that all the other constituent elements of the federation were supposed to suffer the fate of Kosovo and Vojvodina and no one accepted that. That is why we proposed a full confederacy. However, a full confederacy, namely, that we should all know what would be left at confederal level and who would be paying for what, so that all the bills and scores would be clean, and also this proposal included a deadline that we should see whether this would work within a three to five-year period. That is to say, that if this model would work, then we would remain in this confederation and if it did not work, then we would all take our separate paths. However, Milosevic did not accept this. He persistently advocated what he allegedly called a modern and firm federation, but in this way, he was actually showing that he was not interested in any kind of Yugoslavia. That he was only interested in a Greater Serbia and later on, time proved this to be true. When Slovenia was given the right to leave Slovenia, when the army withdrew from Slovenia, all of this showed that something else was taking place. Namely, that Yugoslavia was being dismembered and that a Greater Serbia was to take place where Yugoslavia was ravaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You mentioned this about Slovenia withdrawing from Yugoslavia. After Slovenia declared its independence, did the JNA intervene there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Formally, the army did not intervene because Slovenia had declared its independence, but they found a pretext because Slovenia had established its own customs and tariffs or rather its customs checkpoints at the borders. In this way, the Yugoslav customs was no longer operative. So the central customs asked the federal government and the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, to establish customs control and I think that it was in a benign way that he asked for the assistance of the army, if necessary. However, the army, instead of assisting there at the border crossings, they left their barracks with their tanks and they started establishing their own checkpoints at the borders. The Slovenians established their own control. They fought back. There was a conflict, a war, that that went on for 10 days and I also tried to contribute to bringing these conflicts to an end. I could not take the highway, so I had to take some small country roads to Ljubljana and, together with Milan Kucan, I talked to the top military people and finally we convinced them that it would be the best for the war to stop and that the Territorial Defence of Slovenia and the army should go back to their barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time period when the JNA was involved in Slovenia, on 30th June, did you issue an Order relative to the JNA returning to barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. There was a decision passed by the Presidency previously that the army could remain outside barracks for three months. Those Army units were outside already, so I did not need a new decision. On the basis of the already existing decision, I issued orders to the effect that all the army units should withdraw into the barracks. Of course, they did not carry this through. This meant a military coup d'état and after that, neither formally nor factually, did the Army listen to any kind of Presidency. They only listened to Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I could like to show the witness a document which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 102. (Handed). Can you identify this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. I signed this. The date is June 30th and it says that the general staff should stop all military action in Slovenia in keeping with the agreement reached between the leadership of Yugoslavia with the representatives of the European Community, that all military units should withdraw, that all military units should withdraw into barracks throughout the country. Thirdly, I order the general staff of the JNA to urgently withdraw their order on mobilisation, and, forthly, I inform all federal and republican authorities as well as the general public, both home and abroad, that I have been compelled to take this step, because of the persistent prevention of the members of the Presidency of the SFRY from Serbian Montenegro, from allowing the Presidency of the SFRY to be constituted in keeping with the constitution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in what capacity did you issue this Order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I issued this Order in the capacity of Member of the Presidency and Supreme Commander of the Yugoslav Army, because, at that time, according to the constitution, I held that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And was there any compliance on the part of the JNA with the Order that you issued as the legal head of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they laughed. They laughed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, perhaps it might be an opportune time for a short break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Right. We will adjourn until 10.35, so 20 minutes. (10.15 am) (A short adjournment) (10.35 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, we had left off with this Order that you had issued on 30th June. With the intervention of the EC troika, were you able to formally assume the office of President of the Presidency on 1st July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this intervention took place because the Presidency was not constituted. However, the European troika exerted pressure on the Serb bloc and finally I was elected President -- rather, I was confirmed as President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 4th July 1991, did a meeting of the Presidency occur in relation to the fighting that was still ongoing in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that meeting, all of that that was happening in Slovenia was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there any discussion then or any decision taken about the JNA returning to barracks in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main point, that the army should withdraw into the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 8th July, just four days later, did a meeting take place at Brijuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At Brijuni, a meeting was held with the assistance of the European troika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And were Representatives of all of the Yugoslav republics present at that meeting as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that we waited for the Representatives of Serbia and Montenegro for a long time. I do not know exactly now all who was there, but I know that we had a majority and that we could pass decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What was the outcome of this meeting? Was there any decision reached in regard to the situation in Croatia and Slovenia and particularly in relation to the independence of those two republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the main item on our agenda. Namely, the European troika insisted on that, that the Croatian and Slovenia decisions on independence should not be implemented within a three-month period. No one had objected in any way to the right of Croatia and Slovenia to become independent; however, there was simply this proposal to try by political means, to avoid conflicts within a three-month period and to try to avoid resolving problems by exerting pressure and force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was the effect of this decision to take away Croatia and Slovenia's independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No mention was made of that. It was only the implementation that was postponed. However, all the results remained because after all, that decision was reached legally, both in Slovenia and in Croatia, so it was quite clear that if a solution could not be found within this three-month period, that these decisions would remain in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. I kindly request that the witness does not provide expertise on who becomes independent and when and how in Yugoslavia. Yesterday we agreed that he would testify only on his role. I heard a whole lot of insults at the expense of the of my state, that he was an epileptic or what have you. It seems that I am defending Slavko Dokmanovic for one single day. This witness was brought in as the President of the Presidency to see what happened. But to question him about Kosovo, about Vojvodina and I do not know what all and that, we are not talking about the subject at all. I have nothing against him. He is answering the questions that are put to him. Now, he is being asked who had become independents and how. We said that this is a question for expertise. So I kindly ask that he is asked only those questions that he knows about, not whether elections were legal or not. That is not for him to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: First of all, the issues on Kosovo and Vojvodina, all of this relates to the dissolution of Yugoslavia and that is why all of that is relevant to these proceedings. It goes to international armed conflict and not to what happened in Vukovar on 20th November, but the broader picture. In terms of -- sorry. I lost my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The question of Croatian independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you very much. In relation to this, he is not talking about any legal conclusions. He is not putting forth this. He is talking about decisions that were made there, that he participated in, and that he participated in discussions and how these decisions were reached and what these decisions were. Again, the legal conclusions as to the effect of those actions by the participants in these conferences, that is for the court and the court alone, so we are not asking a legal opinion, but what more or less was discussed and what discussions he participated in as an individual and as President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila, I must say, your objection is overruled, because I find what the Prosecutor just said is quite appropriate. He is trying to have the general picture and the background to what happened with regard to the effects which are before this court and it will be for the court finally to make legal findings. Of course, the witness will refrain as much as possible from making any legal statements or giving legal definitions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, thank you. Subsequent to this conference at Brijuni, was there a meeting on 18th July in which the issue of withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia came up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. For me, the proposal of the top people of the army and the agreement of Serbia to put this on the agenda, that is the withdrawal of the army from Slovenia and Croatia, all that came as a surprise to me, because if the Yugoslav Army was fighting for the survival of Yugoslavia, it was illogical for me that it would withdraw from Slovenia. In other words, I understood what it was all about. I did not vote in favour of this proposal, but I presented a certain proviso. If the Yugoslav Army is withdrawing from Croatia and from Bosnia-Herzegovina too, then I am going to vote for the withdrawal from Slovenia as well, because I was afraid that this Army, parts of the army, would go into Croatia and into Bosnia-Herzegovina and reinforce those forces that are opposing the legal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the months of July and August of 1991, what was happening in the Krajina region of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Krajina, there was also a referendum. I do not know exactly what the date was. We thought that it was not legal. Namely, it was not held according to any regulations of the Republic of Croatia, although it was on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Secondly, it was strictly a national referendum. This kind of referendum is not possible because decisions were to be passed on the territory. If there is any kind of referendum, then all the citizens from that territory would have to vote, including those who were expelled from that territory. However, they did not appear at this referendum and that referendum did not have any legal effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In the Krajina region, were more areas coming under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that more and more areas were coming under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army, which had actually become the Serb Army. This was only an excuse, that the conflict between two warring parties would be resolved by the army placing themselves in between. However, the army was not standing between the two parties. They were covering the territory that was supposed to become part of a Greater Serbia subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection again, your Honour. These are conclusions. This is not testimony. These are conclusions that a Greater Serbia is being created, that the army is taking this.
