These are conclusions. This is unacceptable. Sorry. But I am not going to protest any more. You decide any way you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I have the feeling that the witness is making statements, giving his own assessments of historical facts. You may contest his assessments later on, but it is a fact that he is pronouncing on facts, on historical facts as seen by him. So I do not know there is any impropriety going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might as well, at this time, the gentleman was holding the position as Commander-in-Chief of the military. Whether in fact he was actually able to exert control or not, he was certainly in a position to gather information and to speak to persons which we will go into in more detail in just a moment. After these areas in Krajina and other areas of Croatia came under Serb control, what was happening to the Croatian civilians who were living there? Were they allowed to stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the civilians were expelled. Many of them were killed too. Many villages were burned to the ground and many people also remained there under very difficult conditions. That is, according to the information that I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During this time period, did you have occasion to discuss these issues and bring these particular points about civilians being killed and expelled to the attention of the minister of Defence, Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked about that, both to Veljko Kadijevic, as the Minister of Defence, at my request, in his office, and also I talked to Borisav Jovic, the Serb Representative in the Presidency and I must say that when the so-called Krajina asked for independence from Croatia, I talked about this to Milan Babic as well, the President of this so-called Krajina, and I said that they were cheating him, that Borisav Jovic and Milosevic were cheating him. These Croatian territories would not become part of Serbia. He was repeating what Milosevic had been saying, namely, that all the Serbs had the right to live in the same state and that they could carry out this right by way of a referendum, although it is well known that the Badinter Commission came to the conclusion that the republics have the right to secede, not peoples, and that is the way it ultimately turned out to be. So I told him that it would be better for them to solve their problems in Croatia rather than in Belgrade. Babic did not exactly listen to me. He said that both of us would live to see all of this becoming Serbia and I said, "No way." It is not only that they would not have Serbia in Croatia, but that he would not have a dentist's office, because he was a dentist in Croatia. As far as Veljko Kadijevic is concerned, I asked him whether he actually saw what was happening, that the army was becoming fully Serb and that they were taking the territory which Garasanin and the member of -- and the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts had called for, namely, that a Greater Serbia was being created and that he had nothing to do in this context, that he was a Yugoslav general and that when he completed this job, others would come in, Serb generals, and there would be no place for him there, just like for any other Yugoslav general. Unfortunately, we could not agree on this and later he published a book in which he confirmed what I am claiming now, that they allegedly were defending Serbs, but actually establishing a new boundary that was supposed to be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any steps ever taken by General Kadijevic or by Borisav Jovic to stop these practices of expulsions of Croatian civilians and the killing of civilians during JNA military actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think there perhaps were some cases where the army had a, so to speak, milder treatment of the population, attitude to the population, but where the army did appear, there also followed some renegade groups, which at the -- at the hands of which the people were terrorised greatly, but the army did not oppose this. When all is said and done, actually, the Army was covering this entire area and the Republic of Croatia was unable to establish its own control on account of that Army and with the great force which it had, the army was in fact protecting this renegade authorities that were doing something which no state can allow and accept in its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with General Kadijevic the issue of how the JNA was fighting for Yugoslavia after Slovenia had been let go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a lot of such conversations as I have already indicated at my own initiative, because not a single general came to see me and I claim that precisely the exit of Slovenia was an example, a case in point, which demonstrated that neither the army nor Serbia were interested in Yugoslavia, because if Slovenia was let go and Slovenia was let go, because there is no autochthone Serbian population in Slovenia and it was impossible to organise coverage in terms of territory of all the Serbs, homogenisation of the Serbs in that territory for that purpose, so I claimed that precisely the leaving of Slovenia was proof that nobody in the army or in Serbia wanted a Yugoslavia. The mission of the Army was to take as much territory as possible and, of course, this is a top-heavy, huge mechanism and it had to be financed, that army, and they were interested in as wide as possible a territory to sustain that army. It was the professional requirement -- request of the officers of the army personnel which were supposed to find such sources of livelihood and Serbia herself was interested in gaining as much space as possible upon the model of an ethnic state and ethnic boundaries. Kadijevic gave me this explanation. He said, "Slovenia can go, but you will see in a matter of years Slovenia will be applying in writing to return to Yugoslavia".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were all of the top generals and admirals in the JNA at that time Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all of them were Serbs. There were three generals who accepted the new relations and who thought, when all is said and done, that they had been with the JNA for quite a long time and had sought to find their places there so that several Croats remained on the opposite side. General Jurjevic, General Brovet -- Admiral Brovet. There were some, but clearly they had chosen another option.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Below this very top level of leadership, did any certain ethnic group or groups predominate in the officer corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the officer corps, there generally predominated the Serbian ethnic group for quite a number of years, and we actually had conflicts in that corps in 1991, upon which the Croatian Spring movement was actually crushed. As an example, I can use an example in my own municipality, when most of the population had been with the partisans during the national liberation war and there was a negligent number of Ustasha and when young men were sent to military schools or for military training, there would be written in their CVs that their parents had been in the enemy's army and thereby they were eliminated. They were deprived of this possibility of joining the army. Since their parents actually had been with the partisans since 1941 and 1942, they were such people, but it was written in their CVs that their parents had been with the enemy army, and this was how they were eliminated from the ranks of the army. We raised objection to this, but we did not manage to shift the balance of forces because there were claims by them that the Croats and the Slovenes, because they were the most developed republic, did not simply wish to join the army, and the Albanians, because they are underdeveloped on the other hand, did not wish to join the army, so that nobody but the Serbs had that privilege of wanting to join the army. Clearly, after the dismantling, the disintegration of Yugoslavia, people went their separate ways, the Croats to Croatia, the Slovenes to Slovenia, the Muslims to Bosnia. The majority that remained were Serbs. The Macedonians, of course, went to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think there is a minor point that needs to be corrected in that. I am not sure if it was a mistranslation or a misstatement. But it indicated after Croatian Spring in 1991. I believe that should be 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1971, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During the course of July, had fighting intensified in Croatia? July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had intensified because the ranks of the Yugoslav Army also joined in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness a document that we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 103 and ask if you can identify this. (Handed). I must apologise to the court. We do not have an English translation of this document at this time. We will supplement it as soon as possible and we would mark that as Prosecutor's exhibit 103A. At this time, perhaps if the witness can look at it and see if you can identify it, first of all. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. That is a press release, a communiqué of July 26th of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and it contains precisely one of the decisions on a cease-fire and the cessation of all hostilities, the launching of talks on the modalities of that cease-fire and a decision on the disarming of illegitimate paramilitary formations and armed groups and also the units of the Yugoslav armies should go back to barracks. It also continues. That is the part where I disassociated myself from the decision: "The cease-fire requires that the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia are not sent to the crisis areas where the population is a majority Serb population." I did not accept that particular segment because I -- it was my view that the Croatian police and all the other mechanisms, of the country of Croatia that is, had the right to function throughout the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where was the village of Kijevo located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kijevo is situated in the immediate vicinity of Knin and the Croatian Ministry of the Interior adopted, if that is what we are talking about, a decision to establish a military -- a police station in Kijevo because that particular area remained uncovered by police protection, especially because the police station in Knin had remained outside the control of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to the village of Kijevo in late August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that village was burnt down and clearly a role in the burning down of the village and the expulsion of all the villagers was played by the Yugoslav Army from the Knin garrison, which at that time was headed, I believe, by Colonel Ratko Mladic. The burning of the village -- participating in the burning of the village and the expulsion of the villagers were also some paramilitary formations, but also the logistics and the tank support was given by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did you participate in a conference which was held in The Hague in early September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That session was held in this city. It was attended by all the Members of the Presidency and all the Presidents of the Presidencies, i.e. the Presidents of the Yugoslav republics. That was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this conference, were any proposals offered by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lord Carrington offered very concrete proposals. Most of the participants in the conference agreed with him. Namely, it was quite clear the conference itself -- and it was also so noted by Lord Carrington -- that the former constituent elements of the Federation had gained independence and that they were able, each on its own, to choose their further options and degree of independence and with whom they wished to associate in the future, but he also said that in exercising that right, one had to take into consideration the need to protect collectivities, to protect the rights of groups and entities whose parent state turned out to be a different one from their ethnic group. That parent state would be entitled to take care of its minorities living elsewhere, which normally meant that that right would also be enjoyed by the Albanians in Kosovo. However, Milosevic would not accept that and I believe that he was the only one who did not accept it. Even Bulatovic accepted this on behalf of Montenegro and his minister, whose name I believe was Samarjic, the Minister of Foreign Affairs that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: There were a number of meetings which had taken place after 25th June in an effort to broker a peace, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At these meetings what was the role of the Presidents of the various republics -- Milosevic, Tudjman, Kucan -- as opposed to the Representatives of the Yugoslav Presidency? What had the more dominant role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Members of the Presidency played no role at all any more, because the actual situation was that Yugoslavia was not functioning, that it did not exist, that the republics had gained independence, so the Members of the Presidency did not participate any longer in any political consultations as to how to go about addressing political problems that we were faced with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 11th September, did you issue a decision again calling for a return to barracks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Then, and again invoking my right from the previous decisions of the Presidency, I demanded for the army to get back into barracks and they informed me of their offer, the relevant factors, and it was particularly worrisome that the army decided to act on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness a document which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 104 and, again, our apologies to the court: there is no English translation of this. One will be provided subsequently. That would be marked under the number of 104A. (Handed). Mr. Mesic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. This is my Order, where in the introductory section I speak about what had transpired before I passed that Order and where I mention that the Army is wholly opposing Croatia -- not in fact opposing, but it was bombarding Croatian towns and villages, and I am mentioning the actual places where that had happened. And then it culminates in the Order which says that all the units are to withdraw to their barracks within 48 hours and that those units which, aided by renegade groupings, have seized the area of the municipality of Beli Manastir should withdraw from that area within 72 hours. As of the moment of the disclosure of this Order in the media, all military commanders who fail to heed this order and to comply with it, to execute the order of the Presidency of the Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia about the withdrawal of the army into barracks will be outlawing themselves. The withdrawal of the JNA units into barracks, the disbanding of the so-called Territorial Defence, which is -- which has been illegally mobilised, because it is not supported by a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY, will mean creating the conditions for the peaceful resolution of the crisis and with a democratic dialogue between all the relevant factors. It is only by the withdrawal of the army into barracks that it will be possible to ensure the rule of law and the operation of all the institutions of the state. I signed this on September 11th of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did the JNA comply with your order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army did not execute this order. Actually, their pressure only intensified and their involvement only intensified; their efforts only intensified in order to topple the established order in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In this Order, you had mentioned that the JNA should withdraw from the area of Beli Manastir. What is the region around Beli Manastir between the Drava and the Danube rivers known as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Baranja. I have to explain a bit why Beli Manastir was mentioned, because this entire exercise, in the military sense, was undertaken by the Yugoslav Army, even without any support to speak of on the part of the renegade elements, because there were not too many of those either there. So all this devastation and the occupation itself, was in fact carried out by the Yugoslav Army and I believe it was a Novisad garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was the Baranja region predominantly Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none of the areas, but Vojvodina and Serbia had a majority Serbian population. On the contrary, the population was Croatian, the majority of the population were Croats, according to the last, that is to say, 1991, census.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that Baranja is relatively close to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite close to Vukovar and it is more or less a similar, geographically speaking, area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the end of September and into the first week of October, where were you located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During that period, were there any efforts to call meetings of the Presidency in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to call a meeting of the Presidency. I got in touch with all the Members of the Presidency, but I was physically prevented as the Head of State. I was unable to reach the place on a plane because all the airports had been blocked by the Yugoslav People's Army and I could only come using a vehicle of the Yugoslav People's Army or with means which were in the service of the Yugoslav People's Army, and therefore I could not just simply agree to coming to Belgrade in any other way, except by being granted free passage, and those who were sitting in Belgrade then took advantage of this situation and the further action escalated. Namely, they joined in the military coup d'état which was in the making.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness a document which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 105 and ask if you can identify this. (Handed). Again, your Honours, there is no English translations. That would be marked as exhibit 105A. Can you identify this document? It is actually two documents, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document where I inform in writing Anton Stari, the General Secretary of the Presidency of the SFRY in Belgrade, on September 30th, that I was protesting against the convocation of a session which would be convoked by anyone else and I stated that I would accept if I was provided passage to attend the session and I say, "Please be so kind also as to inform the Members of the Presidency that the President has been prevented for a long time in discharging his duties, because the Yugoslav People's Army is preventing him from coming to Belgrade. Namely, the convoking of a Presidency session at that time, though actually I was not prevented, because they were invoking my -- being prevented from discharging my duty as the reason for their failure to convoke a Presidency session. I was not prevented. I was not personally prevented because of my own incapacity or illness, so I wanted that stated clearly, that I informed the rest of the Presidency that if they were to respond to an illegally-convoked session, they would also be aligning with those who were carrying out the military coup d'état. And that is what I stated clearly in this communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what is indicated in the newspaper article that is attached to the rear of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Stejpan Mesic, according to the request of the Serbian bloc, is to call a Presidency session. In his statement given to the Hjena, the President of the Presidency of the SFRY, Stejpan Mesic, asked how he commented the day before yesterday's statement, released from the session of the rump Presidency held in Belgrade, in which, inter alia, it was requested for a session of the Presidency to be convoked as a matter of utmost urgency, 'and that if he continues to be incapacitated, unable to attend, and if conditions which are prescribed under the rules of procedure for the convoking of a Presidency session should indeed prevail, then the session should be chaired by the Vice-President of the Presidency.'". This is what he said: "In view of the fact that the army has blocked the roads and the air traffic routes, I am unable to call a session in Belgrade, but only Zagreb or Ljubljana or any other city, which I can reach by road.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, I would like to show you now another set of documents which relate to this same time period and I will mark this as Prosecutor's exhibit 106. Again, there is no English translation. That will be submitted as 106A. If you can identify these documents and perhaps summarise them for the court. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first page, the Presidency of the SFRY, again, addressed to the Secretary General, Belgrade, dated October 2nd 1991 and signed by me. I note -- I acknowledge receipt of an invitation which convokes the 144th session of the Presidency and I also state in my communication that I consider it an illegally convoked session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The second document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the original document. It is quite okay. The second document is also dated October -- no, sorry. This is a copy. October 1st is the second one. This is Anton Stari informing me about the agenda, the session at which we were going to discuss some topical question from the area of general national defence. That is this convocation of session No. 144, with the agenda enclosed. That is the one which I distanced myself from in the previously shown document, because I did not recognise the illegality of that invitation and that is the invitation to that Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe, just for the sake of clarity, that was the third document in that group, was it not, if you can look again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, the third document is the agenda itself and the invitation sent to me by the Secretary General, but clearly under the influences of the Vice-President, who assumed upon himself some powers which he did not actually have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If you can look at the second document, the middle document that was in that packet, and summarise what is indicated in that one? I am sorry, I believe you have indicated that that is a copy of the first document; is that correct? I apologise. That was my mistake. At this time, I would like to show you documents which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 107 and see if you can identify this document. Your Honours, in this one, there is an English copy as well as the one in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an original document. There is an English translation too. I am addressing the President of the United States of America, George Bush. I am informing him about the ultimatum issued by the Yugoslav People's Army to the Republic of Croatia as evidence that the army is acting autonomously and extra-institutionally. I also inform President Bush that the Yugoslav Federation no longer exists, that the Army is preventing me from coming to Belgrade. I am informing him about the continued aggression of Serbia and the Yugoslav People's Army, which is no longer Yugoslav, which has become Serbian. I ask for this new reality in our part of the world to be recognised. I also state that the Serbian regime of Slobodan Milosevic toppled the Yugoslav Federation and I conclude that it is only through the recognition of the new entities within their boundaries that the war can be stopped, as well as destruction and a war that could spread to the rest of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show you a document I am going to mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 108, which appears to be the same letter directed to the Secretary General of the UN, Javier Perez de Cuellar. (Handed). Can you tell me if in fact that is the same letter directed to Mr. Perez de Cuellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is a letter to the Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Perez de Cuellar, the text is the same, but I must add to this that I visited, as President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the United Nations and I spoke of what was happening and I said what I think would happen on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Over there, I was asked whether one of the possible solutions was the following, to sacrifice part of the territory for the sake of peace and to cede this territory to Serbia and I said, "What part of Croatia's territory?" They said, "That part that borders with Serbia." I explained that the majority population there was Croat and that the majority Serb population is over 500 kilometres away in Knin and that this was impracticable and impossible and that this would be a reason for war. The situation evolved as presented here. A brutal war broke out and in this letter, I informed Perez de Cuellar about the results of the effective non-intervention of the international community. Had the international community deployed its forces along the border between Croatia and Serbia and the border between Bosnia and Serbia, as I had proposed, there would have been no war, and a peaceful solution would have been found and I concluded that the international community and European and world mechanisms became inoperative in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Despite these protests that you were lodging, both with the other Members of the Presidency and with world leaders, did the meetings of the Presidency go on in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Presidency never met again. Our last two meetings were precisely here in The Hague, where we all met together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did a group of members within the Presidency meet forming, in effect, a rump Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but this was no longer the Yugoslav Presidency, according to the constitution. This was the group that we had called the Serbian bloc between ourselves, that is to say Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo and Vojvodina; they had proclaimed themselves a relevant factor and they excluded the others. They continued to operate as this rump Presidency. Their decisions were not binding on anyone and they continued with this illegitimate activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did this rump Presidency, to your knowledge, authorise expanded action by the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely. Afterwards, the army drew conclusions from the decisions that were passed by this rump Presidency, but in this way, the army leadership only continued their coup d'état activity, because it was quite clear to them that everything they were doing was only implementation of a military coup d'état.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: On 7th October 1991, were you at the Presidential Palace in Zagreb, Banski Dvori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is yet more evidence that the army was involved in a coup d'état. Namely, from Zagreb, I called Ante Markovic in Belgrade who was Prime Minister of Yugoslavia. I asked him to come to Zagreb so that we could try to analyse the situation that had emerged. The state Presidency was in a state of blockade. The Executive Council, that is the government, was also in a blockade and also the Federal Parliament. Everyone was at a standstill and that is why I invited the Prime Minister to meet with me in Zagreb. I talked to him on the telephone. I said that I would meet him the next day at 10 am. At 11 am, President Tudjman would talk to Ante Markovic, and at 12 o'clock there was to be a luncheon. Ante Markovic accepted this itinerary. We talked on the phone and I simply did not take into consideration the fact that the phone was bugged. Anton Markovic came to Zagreb. We had a meeting. He has his meeting with Tudjman. We were having lunch and an hour later, we went back to President Tudjman's office and at that point, rockets fell on Banski Dvori, exactly on the place where we had been having lunch. My conclusion was that the army wanted to kill me and, in this way, to bring the Vice-President to power legally, because there would be no President. The murder of Ante Markovic was supposed to make it possible for his Deputy Prime Minister, Aca Mitrovic from Serbia, to become Prime Minister legally. And if Franjo Tudjman were killed, there would be chaos in Croatia because the new government was not fully constituted as yet. That is probably what they had in mind. However, fortunately, none of this had succeeded. We withdrew from Banski Dvori into shelter. A man was killed there. There was quite a bit of destruction and in the shelter, we agreed on the following: that I would go to the Benelux countries to ask for recognition of Croatia and that Anton Markovic should go to Austria and to ask the Republic of Austria for the same thing. I did my job and I received assurances that we would be recognised. Later, all of this was accelerated. It is precisely this attack on Banski Dvori that speeded up the recognition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was this attack launched by a JNA aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was done very professionally. Their targeting was excellent, but, luckily for us, we were not at the place where they knew that we would be having lunch, otherwise I would not be here as a witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any other air attacks launched during this time period on the city of Zagreb itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were attacks on the city of Zagreb from other areas, areas that were under the control of the Yugoslav Army and Milan Martic, with his groups. Zagreb was attacked several times. There were casualties. There was quite a bit of destruction in the streets of Zagreb and quite a few buildings were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That was in 1995, though, that you are referring to, the attack launched by Mr. Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I just wanted to say this in a sequence. That these attacks went on until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time in October when the JNA launched an action against the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was an action of the Yugoslav Army after all. Some reservists from Montenegro had joined in too. It was the first time in the history of the city of Dubrovnik that it was attacked. Its walls were there for hundreds and hundreds of years, but this was the first time that it was attacked in such a brutal way. In the vicinity of Dubrovnik, in Konavli, there was total devastation. Many human lives were lost and there was major destruction, because the Yugoslav Army had completely encircled Dubrovnik, from sea and land. Dubrovnik had no way out and I decided to try to break through this blockade with a convoy and to bring assistance to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did Dubrovnik have any significant Serb population living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs lived there as individuals, as Croatian citizens, but there were not any Serbs that covered a certain part of the territory of the area of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were Serbs in the majority in the population there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dubrovnik? No, no. It is insignificant in terms of their presence in Dubrovnik, but in Konavli that was razed to the ground, there were not any Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were there any large military installations in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, none. This is a cultural centre with major historic monuments. It is a tourist area. There was no reason to attack Dubrovnik. No military reason to attack Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document I will mark now as Prosecutor's exhibit 110 and ask if you can identify this and also I would show you Prosecutor's exhibit 111.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 109, you are forgetting one number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, 109 and 110 would be these two exhibits. Again, I believe it is the same letter (handed) addressed to Mr. Perez de Cuellar and to President Bush of the United States. Both of these letters are in English. Is it possible for you to identify what these documents relate to, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both are authentic documents. It is about the attack on Dubrovnik. I described what happened there and of course I asked for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At approximately the same time that you wrote these letters, do you recall writing another letter to Mr. Perez de Cuellar talking about the situation in general of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly. Because it is precisely the United Nations that I wished to inform about the escalation of the war and I wanted to show that I was right when I asked for the protection of borders and the prevention of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness another document, which I will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit 111. If you can just briefly identify this document and then indicate to the court what is said in it. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a letter dated October 4th and I am writing to Mr. Perez de Cuellar, Secretary General of the United Nations, and I am telling him that Veljko Kadijevic formally declared war on the Republic of Croatia. I said that it was the survival of the Croatian people and the Croatian state that are at stake and the Air Force and the naval forces are engaged in order to protect the Serb regime and -- the annex to this letter is not here, but I sent this declaration of war by General Kadijevic as an annex to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At the end of October, did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sorry. At the end of October, did you undertake an initiative in relation to getting through the naval blockade of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we formed a convoy which was on a peace mission with some 40 ships. The biggest one was Slavja and I was on that ship. We had announced that we would be going to Dubrovnik because we wanted to give encouragement to the people of Dubrovnik so that they would see that they were not on their own, and we also wanted to bring aid to them in terms of food and medicines. The army stopped this convoy; long, painstaking negotiations ensued. The army, notably Admiral Brovet, asked that we go to Montenegro, to Zelenika, where the ships would be checked, because allegedly there were cannons on the ship. I said that cannons were in their heads, that this is a humanitarian mission, this is humanitarian aid, and that we should get through to Dubrovnik, because I thought that they would not sink me and finally, after a lot of wrangling, long negotiations, they let us into Dubrovnik. We unloaded this aid. Some of our people got killed because, at that time, yet another attack on Dubrovnik had started while we were still in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Did there come a point in December of 1991 when you formally resigned from the office of President?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian Parliament had appointed me its representative in the Presidency of Yugoslavia. However, since I came to the conclusion that Yugoslavia no longer existed, I formally resigned in the Croatian Parliament and my resignation was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: During your tenure as President and during the year of 1991, did the JNA obey any of the orders that you issued to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regrettably, I must say that not a single officer, not a single member of the Yugoslav Army -- did not carry out a single order of mine. If I can say this with a certain degree of irony, with the exception of General Vasiljevic. I told him to sit down and he sat down. That is the only thing they carried out during my tenure as President of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions of Mr. Mesic. I would, however, offer exhibits 102 through 111. I would tender those for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to tell you something. I read in a newspaper from Zagreb that they showed me yesterday that I called you the guilty party for the war and that that is why I asked you to come here. I think that you and I have known each other for long enough that you realise that I could not have said something so stupid. Yes, it was in Globus. So please, these last two days, could you tell me exactly when the Presidency of Yugoslavia met in The Hague? When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have the document here. This was mid-September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay and I think the beginning of October if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it possible that this is the 18th October? I will show it to you. Your signature is here too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it here any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is here. On 4th and 5th November, were you in The Hague again? Was there a meeting here again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the first and second session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And a third one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not come to the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So there were three sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I was only at the first two.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In what capacity were you here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the capacity of Member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But it is obvious that the next session was without the Members of the Presidency. That is to say, that these were negotiations held by the Presidents of the Republics. However, the important thing is that you were here on 4th and 5th November in your capacity as President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Member of the Presidency. I am sorry. Not President of the Presidency. My mistake. Quite a few things have been said about you and I have quite a few statements here, so, please, when you say that this is true, then we are going to accept that, but perhaps the rest of it is simply something that was launched by journalists and which is not true, like the one I referred to a few moments ago. We read that, for you, the HDZ is an extremist nationalist party, a hindrance to democracy, which introduced a single way of thinking and which robbed the people; is that what you really meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to look at this in terms of the time period involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, but have you said something like this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This statement of yours calls for clarification. Namely, when the HDZ was established first, when I was its member, when its programme was elaborated, that was a party that was in favour of a multi-party system, for democratisation and a free society. When the balance of political forces in the HDZ changed, I left the HDZ and I became critical of the policy of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is to say, that this statement is from this latter period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from this later period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the meetings between Milosevic and Tudjman in Kavajorjavo. Is it true that you said that after these meetings, obviously there were several such meetings if I understood you correctly, in that context, that Milosevic established Republika Srpska and Tudjman established Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I never claimed that this was agreed in Karadordevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I did not say that either. I said that it happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I did claim that Milosevic established Republika Srpska and that the Croats, supported by the policy of Presidency Tudjman, established Herceg-Bosna on the other part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say the same. Republika Srpska and Republic Bosnia, on the other side, a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In response to the establishment of Republika Srpska, you said that the two of them -- I am referring to Milosevic and Tudjman -- were agreeing on this division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then you testified here as to what Milosevic had proposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did Tudjman answer? That is what I am interested in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tudjman told us what Milosevic had proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did Mr. Tudjman accept this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what he did there. He said that this is what Milosevic was proposing, but what they agreed upon, that is something that we never heard decidedly. Maybe somebody else has this information, but I do not, what was specifically agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You know very well that there some kind of paper napkin on which President Tudjman had made a drawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not in Karadordevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, but this was later in London. I think that is when I last saw you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is when this napkin emerged. I have not identified it. Somebody else has to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If Tudjman and Milosevic had reached some sort of agreement, how come the JNA attacked Dubrovnik when they were in cahoots? It is not logical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not illogical because Milosevic deceived everyone, including the Serbs in Croatia. Namely, he just needed the Serbs as a primer cap. That it was only after the Flash and Storm operations he did not lift a finger to protect the Serbs who had led into war in Croatia rather than against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the Serbs themselves had to lift a finger or two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. He contributed to this policy because Serbia, simply speaking, under the leadership of its radical part, did not look for a solution in Zagreb with the Croatian authorities, but rather always opted for Belgrade and the Belgrade authorities and their say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked this question because if Milosevic and Tudjman had reached agreement, a bargain, reached a deal, at the expense of Bosnia-Herzegovina, why then would the JNA attack Dubrovnik? If they were to reach agreement at the expense of other people, why would they attack Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, in this aggression, this disintegration of Yugoslavia, Milosevic obviously also aspired after deceiving Tudjman too and taking a part of Croatia, not only a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The French say that you whet your appetite by eating. That is exactly the case with Milosevic, but he bit off more than he could chew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have also found a statement of yours and you said that Mate Boban in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in fact conducting Tudjman's policy and he told you, "I do not have a policy of my own. The policy that I am implementing is Tudjman's policy." That is what he said. I only repeated it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that he said that nothing was undertaken in Herceg-Bosna without the knowledge of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there at all any crimes in the territory of Croatia, because it is hard to conclude that from your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not asked by anyone about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But to tell you very clearly, in response to a question, there were crimes and people were not brought to justice on time and it is a pity for Croatia because there were no such trials and I do claim that, had Croatia functioned as a state, observing the rule of the law to the full, today we would not need the Tribunal in The Hague to try our citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is responsible for that situation with the Serbs and Muslims? For the murders of Serbs and Muslims? Is it Tudjman that is responsible in Pakracka Poljana, for instance, for the eviction of Serbs from their apartments and dismissal from their jobs? And we know that that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war was the reason why there was mutual hatred, and collective recriminations were traded by the collectivities. All the Muslims found all the Serbs to blame for their fate and all the Croats as well, and to the Croats it was all the Serbs and all the Muslims that were to blame, and by virtue of things and the logic of war, when it comes to the Serbs, they held all the Croats and all the Muslims responsible for their fate, so everybody was to blame in everybody's eyes. What we needed and what we need now is to individualise guilt and that is to answer your first question, and I advocate the standpoint that guilt should be individualised. We should not accuse anyone in advance. It is up to the court to apportion the blame of everyone and it is only at that point that we should cease having this collective guilt and recriminations and create conditions for normal co-habitation in Bosnia, in Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that it would be very good for the Serbs also to have an individualisation of guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, for something different, talking about President Milosevic. You said that he was to blame for this, for that, and so on and so forth. That he eroded, undermined Yugoslavia, toppled it. Can you perhaps apply the same yardstick to President Tudjman when it comes to crimes against Serbs, especially what followed after the Storm and the Flash operations and the massacre in the Pakracka Poljana and the killing of the Zec family, which was never condemned. Can you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think we have given Mr. Fila a lot of latitude, but he is asking about events that happened in 1995, which are clearly irrelevant to any issue which is being discussed in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, but what year was the bombardment by Martic of Zagreb? It was also in 1995 and you asked a question relating to that. Was that not correct? Was it not in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In response to that, your Honour, I asked and I believe if the transcript is checked, I indicated during this time period, were there any other bombardments of Zagreb? In response to that question, Mr. Mesic had indicated there were attacks launched by Martic. I then clarified that and said, "That was in 1995, was it not?" And then ceased any questioning on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the Prosecutor is right. Actually, this is my vivid recollection and let us try to confine ourselves to that particular period, 1990-91, because the main problem today is whether or not there was an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: About Kosovo or Croatia; we also talked about Kosovo this morning. That is still not the territory of Croatia. I asked, "In 1991, Pakracka Poljana was in 1991." That was when Serbs were also dismissed from their workplaces. Do you believe that? The responsibility of Mr. Tudjman equals that of Mr. Milosevic for the persecution of those people and their dismissal from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not with a single word did I accuse Slobodan Milosevic of a single crime except for his wrong policies and that wrong policy of his actually led to crime and I am accusing him of planning the war, of reckoning into that war, genocide, because he called for an ethnically pure state, and that he called for a forcible change of borders. That is what I am accusing him of. As for Tudjman, I am also accusing him of a wrong policy, and what are the results of that policy is something to be ascertained by other parties. As for the Zec family, I asked for a trial to be conducted because, after all, a man was killed at his own doorstep, his own yard. His wife and his child were also killed. They were killed in the woods near Zagreb. His wife is Marijana Mesic and I had certainly reason for intervening. The case had been started on and I really abhorred the way the proceedings evolved, because those who had confessed to their crimes, both in terms of Pakracka Poljana and the Zec family were acquitted, because the attorney was not present when they were making the confessions. So what was up to me is I tried to do that, but the actual authorities in charge were derelict in their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Tudjman said that there would only be 3 per cent of Serbs in Croatia after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did not hear him right. In view of the concrete circumstances which prevailed and when that was said, and it was in relation to a regulation which was to sector the extents of the rights of the respective ethnic groups, given their numbers and as the Serbs were in excess of 8 per cent, they enjoyed quite different benefits, because of their large number. So, in that context, Mr. Tudjman -- I do not know exactly why you are asking this, but perhaps he should be asked -- that he just said that after this war, it is to be expected that not more than 5 per cent of Serbs would remain now. I do not know why. Whether he thought that they would leave under duress or that they would leave of their own volition. That is not for me to decide. I only quoted his own conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You talked about the rebellion of Serbs, the revolution, the para-revolution, and so on and so forth, in respect to Plitvice, so that some had been apprehended and then released, but there is no need for us to polemicise because I was their Defence counsel. Be that as it may, as regards Mr. Raskovic, who started this SDS creation, creating the SDS, was he received by Mr. Tudjman and what did Mr. Raskovic ask of Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge and, mind you, I also talked to Mr. Raskovic, he asked for cultural autonomy for Serbs in Croatia. He had a number of conversations in that respect with Mr. Tudjman, which I did not attend, but matters escalated to such an extent that at a large scale rally of Serbs in Croatia, Jovan Raskovic called them to rebellion, but not armed rebellion. However, the situation deteriorated and went beyond his aspirations, as it were, and we saw how he ended up in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was a conversation between him and Mr. Tudjman published and publicly mocked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that conversation should not have been published, but it saw the light of day, however. I believe that it is much better, anyway, to conduct talks even for three years than to wage war for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In 1990, the constitutional Croatia was amended after the victory of the HDZ. What happened then to the Serbian people? Or, to go chronologically, according to the 1974 constitution, there were two constituent nations in Croatia: the Serbs and the Croats. What happened after these amendments to the Serbian people in Croatia? As states had been created and Serbia as the parent state of the Serbian people, I am referring to 1990 and from 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it is quite clear that Serbia was also seeking to exercise her right to independence and what Croatia sought was to establish a new system. In that new system, that is to say, in the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, nothing is said about a single one of the nations, of the peoples. There is a preamble -- and most of us here are jurists. It has a preamble and the binding portion of the constitution. The preamble describes the inception of the Croatian state and the contributions of various factors to that inception of the state and the Serbs are mentioned there, that, as a nation and as individuals, they have contributed to the creation of the Croatian state. They are not the only nations or nationalities as we call them, who are mentioned there, but other ethnic groups are also mentioned as having contributed to the creation of the state, but the binding part does not mention individually specifically by name either the Serbs or the Croats or the Muslims or any other nation. It says that Croatia is the state of all its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I ask you, first of all, in the 1974 constitution, that constitution of Croatia specified two constituent nations: the Serbs and the Croats in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. In 1974, that was so. It was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Serbian people in Croatia and the others were referred to as nationalities. What is the situation according to the constitution at the Badinter Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The republics, it is quite decidedly said according to the constitution, had the right to cessation and it was republics having that right of cessation that had associated to form Yugoslavia. Of course, this position was interpreted differently in Serbia, that it was a right that had been consummated, that the republics could no longer separate. Namely, that is a durable right and a right which cannot be consummated in that way, and it was a right vested in the republics to seek independence because they did not form Yugoslavia as nations, as peoples, but only as members of the Croatian state which had associated into the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, the 1974 constitution speaks about the right of peoples to self-determination, not republics. Where? In what Article is it mentioned that republics have that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the constituent elements of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mean peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not peoples. They are just incidentally mentioned. It was republics, but let us not dwell upon this. We can go on for ever and a day discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You say that until 5th December 1991, you were relieved of office or withdrawn from the Presidency of Yugoslavia by decision of the Parliament. I shall read to you something from our papers: "A Croatian Saba recall the President of the Presidency", and then goes on to quote Mesic: "I have discharged my mission. Yugoslavia no longer exists." I shall not read all of this. It is way too long, of course, what was said. Zarko Domljan said: "On that occasion, Mesic had kept his promise. Yugoslavia is no longer." I should like to ask you the following question in regard to that statement of yours, "I have discharged my mission. Yugoslavia no longer exists." Did you say it and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say this in response to your question. I was delegated to Belgrade on behalf of the Croatian Parliament as Member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. First of all as Vice-President and subsequently as President.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that was the only mission that I was supposed to discharge at that post. Since Yugoslavia was no longer, I had no other mission. I had no mission to be a Prosecutor or an attorney in Belgrade. My sole task was to be a Member of the Presidency and to discharge my duties as Member of the Presidency. When that ceased, my task was over. I no longer had anything to do in the Presidency. Only as a migrant worker, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I was getting at something else. I wish to remind you of this statement because I want to ask you to explain to the court. Why there was a stop? Why did you not become President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? Why did they not want to elect you President? Because you had said something, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, these are speculations. These are speculations of Bora Jovic and of course his mentor. Allegedly, I had said that I would be the last President of Yugoslavia. When I went to Belgrade, the function was no long -- the Federation was no longer functioning. Nothing was functioning in the state. All the republics were dissatisfied with their status, the provinces included. I think it would also be logical if the provinces got the right to say, by way of a vote, what they wanted and what they did not, but regrettably they did not get this right. In that situation, I was getting ready to go to Belgrade where everyone sought a reconstruction of Yugoslavia. I have a sane mind, so I came to the logical conclusion, that in this constellation, in this mechanism that was established, I am probably the last President. Everyone else will either come to a confederal Yugoslavia or there will simply no longer be a Yugoslavia. I simply came to this logical conclusion. And I was right. Not a single one was elected any more. It was not through my will, but through the operation of these political forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: However, did you state that you would be coming to Belgrade to be the last President of Yugoslavia? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. In response to a journalist's question, I said that I think I am going to be the last President of Yugoslavia in this constellation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Because it was not functioning as you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to read something to you, please. You wrote a book, in all fairness, "How We Toppled Yugoslavia". When you say "we", it is probably you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I did not contribute to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We all contributed to it together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps I can even agree to that. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you said that -- I mean, you have taken the oath when you came here, right? When you came to Belgrade, and 18 million Yugoslavs, myself included, heard you take the oath. Would you read it to me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why not? Do you want me to read it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are going to say whether I -- "I state that I am going to struggle for the protection of the sovereignty, independence... "I solemnly declare that I am going to strive for the protection of the sovereignty, independence and integrity of the country and for the realisation of the power of the working class and all working people, that I will strive for the attainment of brotherhood and unity and the equality of rights of nations and nationalities, for the development of a social self-management society, for the exercise of common interests of the working people and citizens of the SFRY, and that I will abide by the constitution of the SFRY and federal laws and conscientiously discharge my duties." And you buried that state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not bury it. I must say that I honoured my oath, my constitutional oath, but Yugoslavia was no longer there; I could not help it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Or you did not want to help it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If a person has been drowning for three days, you cannot resuscitate him. So, accordingly, no effort of mine could have saved Yugoslavia. It was simply a waste of time, because other factors had destroyed Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But why did you not resign? That is an honourable thing to do. You deceive people. You make them believe that you are going to do something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is honourable to say, "This Yugoslavia is falling apart and I am leaving."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not exactly that way, because then somebody else would have come to my place and he would not have observed the interests of the Republic of Croatia or others and, after all, I had this responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I imagine that you are not the only person who can protect the interests of Croatia. Probably Tudjman could have protected the interests of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to protect the interests of those who sent me to Belgrade, and I think that I did my job conscientiously. Namely, I had persistently been asking for the following. That the state mechanisms should function. That the army should get out of political decision-making and that political problems should be resolved in peace. And, later on, it became obvious how, for example, the Chets and the Slovacs could work things out in a civilised manner. Had the JNA not been arming the Serbs in Croatia, had there not been for the ambition to break up Bosnia, had it not been for this ambition to change borders, of course a confederal concept could have been reached in peace, or the country could have broken apart -- but in peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: For example, why did you not give cultural autonomy to Vaskovic? Was it indispensable to get the Serbs out of the constitution precisely at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot object to me on the count of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But this is a different matter, this is not part of this process. How do you interpret the statement made by Zarko Domljan? Mesic had kept his promise that he would be the last President of Yugoslavia. That is the promise you made as you were going to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably Zarko Domljan did not understand what I said when I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said, as you were speaking of Kosovo, that 90 per cent of the population of Kosovo is Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that in Croatia, there are 10 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: More or less. The figures are not very accurate, but never mind. Is Kosovo part of Serbia or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kosovo became part of Serbia because, in the Second World War, an agreement was reached between Tudjman -- sorry, not Tudjman, Tito and Ilija Holja that there should be an uprising in Kosovo against the Italians and the Germans and that after the war, the status of Kosovo would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But whose was Kosovo before the war? Come on. What state did Kosovo belong to before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was part of the unitary Yugoslavia, but in the Second World War, this Yugoslavia no longer existed. It was built on a different foundation. It could not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, come on. Let us go back to the First World War. Was it not part of Serbia then before the First World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the First World War, it was Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And Kosovo was in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but new subjects came into being in the Second World War. Republics were established and Kosovo, as an area, because Albanian insisted, because of the majority Albanian population, that already in the Second World War it should become part of Albania. And Tito had a different logic. Now it is important to fight against the occupiers and we are going to work out the status of Kosovo after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, finally, after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, after the war, it was in Serbia, but it got a high degree of autonomy. And that province and Vojvodina practically had statehood, because they had one representative in the Presidency like any other republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to the constitution from 1974; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned 2 million Albanians. What percentage of the population of Serbia is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I have not been dealing with Serbia specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: However, since you know so much about Kosovo, you must know about Serbia too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I imagine that Serbia has a population of over 10 million.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, so that is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how many Serbs were there in Croatia in 1991 according to the census? What did you say? And how many Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there were about 700,000, 800,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Together with the Yugoslavs, about 1 million; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is that 10 per cent of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are you saying together with the Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are no part of the -- Yugoslavs were Croats and Yugoslavs were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But most were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not think so. They were from mixed marriages; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not only mixed marriages. There is no point in making a problem out of who the people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, but you said 700,000. Is that 10 per cent of Croatia's population or is it a bit more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, it is about 12 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is even more, but never mind. Now, you talked about the success of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian referendum?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the territory of Vukovar, was there a referendum and was it successful?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am defending a person who has been indicted for Vukovar. I do not know what will happen about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the territory where the referendum was carried out, at that referendum, 84 per cent of the people who took part voted in favour of independent Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I asked you about Vukovar. What about the referendum there? Did they have 50 per cent of the people who voted or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who says that over 50 per cent of the people involved have to vote at a referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A referendum is organised as an entire state territory and in some places, people do not have to vote in the referendum at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. But do you know how many people took part in the referendum in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to the decision of the Parliament, you were recalled. And why did they not discuss then the recall of Kadijevic, Loncar and Markovic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia asked all their citizens after it became independent, after Croatia became independent, and after I left the Presidency, Croatia invited all its citizens to come back to Croatia, regardless of their ethnic background. Many Serbs from state institutions went back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking about the decision passed by your Parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of these people even became ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to the decision of the Parliament, only you are being withdrawn, not Ante Markovic or anyone else. I asked why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, on that occasion, it is only my resignation that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay, I understood that. Now my other question. In view of the composition of the federal authorities, the Prime Minister was Ante Markovic, a Croat. Kadijevic was an officer from Croatia; right? Brovet, okay, he was from Slovenia. Why are judges being withdrawn and the Republic of Ukraine is being --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry. A couple of notes have been passed us by the interpreters asking that you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. At that same meeting on 5th December, the Parliament reached a decision that the government of Croatia should take steps for the implementation for Croatia to sail into international waters, et cetera et cetera -- only then. Why only then? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I am not the representative of Croatia here. I am here --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you are not a representative of Kosovo either, but you know all about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am here as the former President of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am asking you as the former President of Yugoslavia: on 5th December, why did Croatia ask for the launching of such action? I am going to read this to you: "The Parliament of the Republic of Croatia asked the Government of Croatia to start the necessary procedure in keeping with the relevant legislation to include Croatia into international affairs", et cetera, et cetera. Why only then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first occasion when I see President Tudjman, I am going to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, this is the Parliament, the Parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, then I am going to ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Zarko Domljan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am going to ask the current President of the Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Vukovar perhaps have an influence on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would Vukovar have an impact on this? I do not see why.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In order to speed up the decision on recognition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no reason why Vukovar would have an effect on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have quite a few of your signatures here, you know, where you signed different decisions as the President of the Presidency of the SFRY, even after October 1991, on the promotion of officers, et cetera. It is not clear to me why you were doing this and now you are claiming that no one listened to you in that army?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might object. I think that, in all fairness, if he is referring to documents with his signature on them, that he should have the opportunity to view those before he is asked to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I withdraw the question. But certain documents were signed. There is no question about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Remember that I was given promotions of officers and non-commissioned officers to sign, but I did not sign those documents. I also know that I was given documents regarding decorations of men and I did not sign those either. Whether I did sign something prior to those events, and that was published later, I am not really sure, but I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you happen to know when Messrs Loncar, Markovic and Kadijevic seized the discharging of their offices in the federal republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I cannot recall exactly the -- there was so many things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But was that before or after you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After me, after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you make a statement which has been interpreted in various ways on different occasions in our parts, which is that Serbs cannot believe that they brought the right to the land on their peasant shoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a bit oversimplified. I shall repeat it the way I said it originally. In Krajina, in the so-called Krajina, they used to say and write. There was graffiti and also slogans being shouted. "This is Serbia." What I said was that Serbs in Croatia did not bring Serbia to Croatia on their peasant shoes, because when they were coming, they were certainly not coming in patent leather shoes. That was just by way of an explanation. But I also said on that occasion that not even the Croats took away Croatia to Austria on their peasant shoes, because there they are citizens of the Republic of Austria and they could have taken Croatia there in their hearts, but that they were living on Austrian soil and that they were Austrian citizens.
